endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: This gap presents an opportunity for developers to broaden their users by refining workflows, tailoring them to the unique demands of nursing; inpatient care; various subspecialties; emergency medicine; and ancillary providers, like physical therapy.

endorsements.title: Barriers and opportunities of scaling ambient AI scribes for clinical documentation across diverse healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: Early user engagement to tailor interfaces, workflows, and outputs to the realities of clinical practice are necessary.

evidence.title: Feasibility of Tailoring Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ambient Scribes for Intensive Care Unit Rounds: Algorithm Development and Validation
evidence.effect: For M1, correct rose from 57.25% (V1) to 73.80% (V3) and 69.15% (V4); omission fell from 31.60% to 16.85% (V3).
evidence.quote: Iterative improvements to the prompt increased accuracy and reduced errors during phase 1.

evidence.title: Listening to the note: clinician perspectives on ambient artificial intelligence scribes in medical documentation
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported fit of ambient scribe note sections and formats with local documentation needs
evidence.effect: Clinicians reported overlong or underspecified note sections, unfamiliar formatting and perceived loss of voice, creating new work to reconcile AI drafts with local documentation genres. Tailored prompts and onboarding were suggested but not tested.
evidence.quote: Early ambient scribe implementation produced recognizable benefits, but introduced new work to reconcile AI-drafted text with local documentation genres and audience-specific communication.

evidence.title: What do clinicians edit in ambient AI-drafted clinical documentation? A qualitative content analysis
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Need for specialty-specific detail edits in ambient AI drafts
evidence.effect: Thematic analysis found clinicians edited drafts to add medical specialty-specific details, one of 5 main edit types, indicating generic drafts fit specialties poorly.
evidence.quote: The results of our thematic analysis show that most edits can be categorized into one of the following 5 types: to revise factual discrepancies, to add medical specialty-specific details, to express diagnostic certainties, to convert patient expressions into objective assessments recorded in medical terms, and to reorganize or condense content.

evidence.title: Ambient artificial intelligence scribe implementation in inpatient setting
evidence.outcome: Fit of ambient scribe to inpatient workflows and note types; utilization by note type
evidence.effect: Utilization was low (3% overall; 12% of H&Ps, 2% of progress notes, 6% of consult notes). Physicians requested functionality to pull forward or add onto previously generated notes.
evidence.quote: Future development tailored to inpatient workflows is needed to increase adoption as organizations begin to expand ambient AI in this new clinical setting.

commentary.bottom_line: One offline simulation of five ICU rounds cases found that tailored prompts raised correct note content from 57.25% to 73.80% and lowered omissions from 31.60% to 16.85%, but no study has tested tailored workflows or templates in live practice. Three field studies show that generic ambient scribe output fits specialties and inpatient note types poorly, which supports the concern without showing that tailoring resolves it.

perspectives.view: A single level 4 simulation with five cases tests the practice. It was offline, limited to ICU rounds, and too small to give precise estimates, so certainty is very low. The gains in correct content and the drop in omissions favor the recommendation, but indirectness and imprecision leave the effect in live care uncertain.

In the simulation, omissions fell from 31.60% to 16.85% with a tailored prompt, which suggests tailoring may reduce missing content in intensive care notes. Omitted findings can carry into later decisions. About one in six items was still omitted after tailoring, so clinician review of every draft would remain necessary.

Clinicians added specialty-specific details to drafts and described overlong sections, unfamiliar formats, and loss of voice. Among 59 inpatient physicians, the tool was used for 12% of H&Ps and 2% of progress notes. These studies describe poor fit, and none tested whether co-designed templates improve fit, editing burden, or uptake.

Inpatient utilization of 3% among 59 physicians suggests that purchased capacity may go largely unused when the tool does not match local note types. Physicians asked for the ability to build on prior notes. No study reports the staff time or vendor cost of tailoring by specialty and role, so the resource demand remains unmeasured.

None of the studies reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The one test of tailoring used five simulated ICU cases with no patient characteristics reported. Whether tailored templates perform for interpreter-mediated or non-English encounters has not been examined.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested tailored ambient scribe templates or workflows in real deployment. A prospective comparison of tailored and generic templates across specialties, nursing, emergency medicine, inpatient care, and ancillary roles, measuring note accuracy, omissions, editing time, and uptake, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and the single simulation reported no patient characteristics. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence that the gains seen in simulated ICU cases would carry over to their encounters.
